samples.text:
Nowadays, many people decide to use their holidays for doing voluntary work in other countries, for example building schools, teaching children or protecting animals. In my opinion, this is a positive development for both the volunteers and the local communities.

Firstly, voluntary work can help poor communities. In many developing countries, there are not enough teachers, doctors or money for projects like building a clean water system. When volunteers come, they can give their time and skills for free. For instance, a group of volunteers can build a small school in a village in only few weeks, and many children can study there for years.

Secondly, volunteers themselves get a lot of benefits. They can learn about a new culture, a different way of life and maybe some words of the local language. This is much more interesting than lying on a beach in a hotel. Also, they learn to be grateful for what they have at home, and they can develop new skills such as teamwork and problem solving, which is useful for their future career.

However, some people say that volunteering holidays are not always helpful. Some volunteers have no experience, so the work they do is not very good quality. In addition, some companies charge volunteers a lot of money but only small part of it goes to the project.

In conclusion, I believe that doing voluntary work on holiday is mainly a positive development, because it helps communities in need and give volunteers an unforgettable experience. However, people should choose a good organisation and a project that match their skills.
samples.why: Clear positive position · relevant ideas with a simple example · mechanical linking (Firstly, Secondly, However) · adequate vocabulary · errors in articles, quantifiers and agreement that do not impede meaning.

samples.text:
Rather than spending their holidays relaxing on a beach, a growing number of people are choosing to volunteer on projects abroad, such as building homes, teaching English or supporting wildlife conservation. Despite some criticisms of this kind of travel, I believe it is a positive trend.

For communities that receive volunteers, the most direct benefit is practical help. Many projects in developing regions depend on outside labour and funding to succeed, and volunteers often contribute both. A conservation programme, for example, may rely on visitors to monitor endangered species, while the fees they pay help to cover the salaries of local staff. In this way, volunteering can support work that would not otherwise be possible.

The experience is also valuable for the volunteers themselves. Living and working alongside local people gives them a far deeper understanding of another culture than ordinary tourism provides. Many return home with a greater awareness of global issues such as poverty and environmental damage, and some go on to support charities or choose careers in development. The skills they gain, including adaptability and teamwork, are also highly valued by employers.

It is true that the industry has been criticised. Some projects accept volunteers with no relevant skills, for instance allowing untrained visitors to teach in schools for only a week or two, which can do more harm than good. There are also commercial agencies that charge high fees while giving little to the communities. However, these problems show the need for careful choice of project rather than a reason to reject volunteering altogether.

In conclusion, when volunteers choose responsible organisations and suitable projects, their work benefits both local communities and themselves. For this reason, I consider the rise of volunteer holidays to be a positive development.
samples.why: Clear positive position throughout · main ideas extended with specific examples · criticisms addressed logically · effective paragraphing and linking · good range of vocabulary · frequent error-free sentences.

samples.text:
Volunteer tourism, in which travellers spend their holidays working on community or conservation projects overseas, has grown into a substantial industry. The idea is admirable in principle, yet I would argue that, in the form it most commonly takes, it is a more negative development than its popularity suggests.

Its appeal is easy to understand. Volunteers hope to make a tangible difference, and some projects, particularly those involving skilled professionals such as doctors or engineers, undoubtedly do. Participants also gain an insight into unfamiliar cultures and global inequalities that conventional tourism rarely provides, which may shape their attitudes and choices for years afterwards.

The problem is that most short-term volunteers lack the skills the work requires. A teenager who spends two weeks teaching in a village school, with no training and no knowledge of the local language, is unlikely to contribute much to children's learning, and a steady stream of such visitors can disrupt continuity in the classroom. Similarly, construction projects carried out by inexperienced tourists may be of poor quality and may take paid work away from local builders who could have done the job better and more cheaply.

There are also ethical concerns. Because volunteering has become a profitable product, some agencies design projects around the wishes of paying customers rather than the needs of communities. In the worst cases, children in orphanages form attachments to a succession of visitors who then disappear, which can be emotionally harmful. Such arrangements risk treating poorer communities as a backdrop for the personal growth of wealthier travellers.

In conclusion, although volunteer holidays can broaden travellers' horizons and some skilled contributions are genuinely valuable, many schemes deliver little lasting benefit and occasionally cause harm. For this reason, I regard the trend as largely negative, and would suggest that donating to established local organisations is often a more effective way to help.
samples.why: Clear, critical judgement developed with nuance · specific, well-chosen examples · concession integrated naturally · sophisticated cohesion and paragraphing · wide, precise vocabulary · varied structures used with full accuracy.
